messages.author: 27a3a0f42772bb11
messages.subject: Good (but vanilla) hardware configurations
parts:
Simple question that I would have thought had already been discussed, but I cannot find it.
What is a good standard windows (i.e. desktop) hardware configuration for Stan.
By desktop I don't mean budget, but, mainstream (i.e. no custom supercomputers).

More concretely, if I had - say - $5000-6000 to spend on a desktop box, what would be a good way to spend it.
I'm assuming stripped down processors and memory, without gamer graphics systems, etc.

Thanks,

Sean Matthews

P.S., I currently run Stan on a T440 with an i5 processor, and I'm wondering what an upgrade to an i7 processor would bring, if anything.

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Good (but vanilla) hardware configurations
parts:
Hi Sean,

The limiting factor on Windows is the tool chain, not the hardware. This may change with the new version of RTools, but most of the Stan developers are on Mac for this reason.

I don't know if the Intel compiler is much better for Windows. If so, maybe buy the compiler and spend less on the computer?


Daniel

messages.author: f53f4ca2c430170d
messages.subject: Good (but vanilla) hardware configurations
parts:
The difference in speed between a good cpu and a really good cpu is going to be much much less than the difference between a sloppily written model and a carefully parameterized model. So with that amount of money a box with a multi socket motherboard, decent multi core cpu's and over 64 128gb RAM lets you run a dozen chains of different algorithms and still analyze the last round of results.

A lot of modeling problems require completely independent parallel computation (multiple chains, multiple algorithms, multiple data sets), so multiple cores with enough RAM is where you really can make your workflow easier. Also if you're going to spend that amount of money on a desktop find somebody to buy from who can source reliable components, rather than just the best spec as silly stuff like bad RAM can waste much more time than a marginally faster machine will ever save you.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Good (but vanilla) hardware configurations
parts:
Unless you're running more than four chains in parallel, you
really only need a quad-core CPU --- we don't do any parallelization
within a chain (yet, anyway). If you want to explore a whole
lot of models or parameters or whatever, you'll need a cluster.

Linux works well for servers. And I think you can still set up
Windows and have Linux dual boot in case you decide you hate Linux.

Daniel and I have mid-2012 Macbook Pros with 2.3 GHz i7 CPU and 16 GB
of 1600 MHz DDR3 memory. Michael and Andrew have slightly newer
ones, as does Rayleigh.

We have the newer mini trash-can server in the office for unit
and integration tests and longer-running jobs. And then we (and by
that I mean people with more patience for config than me) just
run on the linux cluster at Columbia.

- Bob

messages.author: a2bfdf24157fa01a
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Good (but vanilla) hardware configurations
parts:
I thought I would chime in on this older thread. I have recently been trying to refine my intuition about what affects model speed across different platforms because I recently discovered that my intuition was quite wrong.

Background:

I ran the same model, same data, same random seed on two computers using cmdstan-2.12. The model uses hierarchical shrinkage priors, and matrix operations over 30k data. Both computers were running the same OS (Arch linux), compilers (gcc 6.2), etc. The biggest difference between the two is hardware:

Computer 1 (desktop):
i7-3770 @ 3.7 GHz
24 Gb RAM - DDR3 1033

Computer 2 (laptop):
i5-6200U @ 2.7 GHz
20 Gb RAM - DDR4 2400

Expectation: The large clock-speed advantage of the desktop would give it an advantage. At worse, I expected the clock-speed advantage to outweigh the older architecture and slower RAM and would make the two about equal.

Results: The laptop was 4x faster than the desktop.

I know there are likely some architecture-specific optimizations happening from gcc, but I am curious how large of a difference the memory is making. I have also run this model on a cloud compute server using Haswell chips running at 2.6Ghz, and experienced model speeds between the two above cases. I am very surprised that of all the hardware I have access to, the laptop is the fastest by a large margin. 

I would be curious if anyone else has experienced this.

Matt

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Good (but vanilla) hardware configurations
parts:
Yes, memory's a huge deal. It takes the equivalent of many
CPU arithmetic instructions to move data from RAM into the CPU's
registers (how many depends on relative CPU, cache, memory, and
bus [if any] speed).

If the desktop doesn't have modern CPU architecture
and is still using a frontside bus instead of the adjacent memory,
that adds even more latency.

The other thing to keep in mind is that the clock speed isn't the
only measure of compute throughput. Better prefetch and memory
dispatch are huge as well as the size of the memory cache, and
then there's the matter of floating point performance and parallel
capacity. So you might want to look at benchmarks of those CPUs.

Although the i7 looks to be much faster at arithmetic, your
i5 has higher memory bandwidth (aside from the faster memory).

It will also depend on how much you parallelize. Looks like the i7
has four cores and the i5 only two.

- Bob
